segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul and Timothy, slaves of Christ Jesus, to all the holy ones in Christ Jesus who are in Philippi, together with the overseers and deacons:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I thank my God every time I remember you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: always, in every prayer of mine for all of you, making my prayer with joy,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because of your partnership in the good news from the first day until now,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: being confident of this very thing, that the one who began a good work in you will carry it through to completion, right up to the day of Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It is right for me to think this way about all of you, because I hold you in my heart, since all of you are partners with me in grace, both in my chains and in the defense and confirmation of the good news.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For God is my witness how I long for all of you with the deep affection of Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And this I pray: that your love may overflow still more and more in knowledge and every kind of insight,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that you can discern what matters most, in order to be sincere and blameless for the day of Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now I want you to know, brothers and sisters, that what has happened to me has actually turned out for the progress of the good news,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that it has become clear to the whole imperial guard and to everyone else that I am in chains for Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and most of the brothers and sisters, made confident in the Lord by my chains, dare all the more to speak the word without fear.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some, it is true, preach Christ out of envy and rivalry, but others out of goodwill.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The latter do so out of love, knowing that I am placed here for the defense of the good news;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: the former proclaim Christ out of selfish ambition, not from pure motives, thinking to stir up affliction for me in my chains.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What of it? Only this: in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed, and in this I rejoice. Yes, and I will rejoice,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for I know that this will turn out for my salvation through your prayer and the support of the Spirit of Jesus Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in keeping with my eager expectation and hope that I will be put to shame in nothing, but that with all boldness, now as always, Christ will be exalted in my body, whether through life or through death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For to me, to live is Christ and to die is gain.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if I am to live on in the flesh, that means fruit from my labor—and which I will choose I do not know.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am hard pressed between the two: I have the desire to depart and be with Christ, for that is better by far;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but to stay on in the flesh is more necessary for your sake.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And confident of this, I know that I will stay, and stay alongside all of you, for your progress and joy in the faith,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that your boasting in Christ Jesus may overflow because of me, through my presence with you again.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Only live as citizens worthy of the good news of Christ, so that, whether I come and see you or am absent, I may hear about you that you are standing firm in one spirit, with one soul contending side by side for the faith of the good news,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and in no way frightened by your opponents. This is a sign to them of destruction, but of your salvation, and this is from God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it has been granted to you, for Christ’s sake, not only to believe in him but also to suffer for his sake,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: having the same struggle that you saw in me and now hear of in me.

notes.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and not for a hired servant. Most English versions soften it to “servants.” In the Greek Old Testament “slave of the Lord” was also a title of honor for figures such as Moses and David, and a first-century reader could have heard both the lowliness and the dignity.

The traditional “saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of unusual virtue. Paul uses the word for all the believers in a place, as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others have “God’s people.”

The first word was an ordinary term for a supervisor or official and is plural here, so it does not yet describe a single bishop presiding over a city’s church, as the word “bishop” now implies. The second word ordinarily means a servant or assistant, but here it appears to name a recognized role in the assembly, so “deacons” is kept. What exactly either group did at Philippi is not known.

“Gospel” has become a religious term and the name of a kind of book. The Greek was an ordinary word for the announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations already alternate between “gospel” and “good news.”

The Greek word means having something in common and was used of business partnerships as well as friendships. Here it refers to the Philippians’ active share in Paul’s work, including their financial support (4:15), so “partnership” is used in place of the older “fellowship,” as in many modern versions. The related word in verse 7 is rendered “partners.”

notes.phrase: I hold you in my heart
notes.traditional: I have you in my heart
notes.note: The Greek can also be read “you hold me in your heart,” since both pronouns are in the same case. The word order favors the rendering in the text, which most translations follow, but a minority of versions and scholars take it the other way.

The adjective normally rendered “righteous” or “just” is used here in the everyday impersonal expression “it is right,” meaning proper or fitting. Neither “righteous” nor “just” would be natural English in this construction.

The phrase can mean the fruit that consists of righteousness or the fruit that righteousness produces, that is, conduct flowing from a right standing with God; the Greek does not decide. Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous and just, righteousness and justice), so “righteousness” here covers both being in the right and doing what is right.

notes.traditional: the whole praetorian guard; the palace
notes.note: The Greek is a Latin loanword, praetorium. It could mean a governor’s official residence, as in the Gospels and Acts, or the emperor’s elite guard in Rome. The following “and to everyone else” suggests people, not a building, so most modern translations take it as the guard. The choice is tied to the disputed question of where Paul was imprisoned when he wrote.

Many early manuscripts read “the word of God,” and a few “the word of the Lord.” The shorter reading is the one printed in the Greek text translated here, and the longer forms may be scribal clarifications, though the manuscript evidence for “of God” is strong and editors are divided.

The Greek word can mean rescue from danger or salvation in the full sense, and many modern versions have “deliverance,” understanding release from prison. Paul’s words here match the Greek version of Job 13:16, where Job expects to be vindicated before God, and verse 20 expects this outcome “whether through life or through death.” Many scholars therefore think Paul means his final vindication, not simply his release; the same word is used in verse 28.

notes.phrase: that means fruit from my labor
notes.traditional: this is the fruit of my labour
notes.note: The Greek is compressed and seems to break off mid-sentence. It can also be read as one sentence: “But if living on in the flesh means fruitful labor for me, then I do not know which to choose.” The verb rendered “know” usually means “make known” elsewhere in the New Testament, so “I cannot tell” is also possible.

notes.traditional: conduct yourselves; let your manner of life be
notes.note: The verb comes from civic life and means to live as a citizen and fulfill a citizen’s obligations, though in Jewish Greek it could also mean simply to live by a certain way of life. Philippi was a Roman colony proud of its citizenship, and Paul returns to the image in 3:20. Most commentators think the civic sense is intended, though translations usually render it generally.

Many versions have “one mind”; the Greek word is the one for a person’s life or inner self, and the phrase describes a community acting as if it shared a single self. The preceding “in one spirit” could also be read “in the one Spirit,” referring to God’s Spirit, but the parallel with “one soul” favors the sense of united resolve.

candidates.reason: The plural addressed to mixed congregations recurs in every letter, and versions split between “brothers,” “brothers and sisters” and “brethren,” so it needs one policy.
It is rendered “bishop” or “overseer” across Acts 20:28, 1 Timothy 3:2, Titus 1:7 and 1 Peter 2:25, and the choice carries assumptions about church order.
It ranges from physical rescue to final salvation, and versions vary between “deliverance” and “salvation” in passages like this one, so a default and alternates are needed.
It means bodily life here but sinful human nature elsewhere in Paul, and versions vary widely (“flesh,” “body,” “sinful nature”), so a rule for the neutral sense is needed.
It is a key verb in Philippians and Romans, covering thinking, feeling and settled attitude; renderings vary (“think,” “feel,” “be minded,” “set the mind on”), which hides the repetition.
